new_statements.rule_in_words: In the traditional (reading-tradition) pronunciation of Talmudic Aramaic, word stress falls on the penultimate syllable; proclitic prepositions and conjunctions are unstressed. A subset of words (derived-stem verb forms with 'thrown-back' final vowel, § 231.5, and forms with syncope of the penult vowel, § 646.2) are pronounced with antepenultimate stress. Modern support (hedged): Bar-Asher Siegal 2013 §4.1 attributes JBA apocope of final vowels to a historical shift of stress from ultima to penult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Levias: antepenultimate accent in a number of cases (traditional pronunciations like NQBRTA/'ISHTN/.. with penult-vowel syncope, § 646.2; retrocession of the accent to the antepenult in derived conjugations and by analogy in Qal, § 231.5); prefixed prepositions and conjunctions unaccented. Margolis 1910 § 7 (p. 15) dissents: he formulates no separate rules and presupposes the Biblical Aramaic accentuation, allowing that 'a shifting of the accent did take place' without effect on the vocalization; his § 5 (pp. 14-15) explains bar, 'at(t) by 'recession of the accent to the penultimate'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, in the 'traditional pronunciation' (reading tradition of the Talmud c. 1900, i.e. the European tradition); not an attested ancient prosody. Sentence-accent contractions are treated separately by Margolis § 6. Kutscher (Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Aramaic', Babylonian Aramaic phonology (4)) only says the accent 'was rather strong; its position was apparently different from the one known to us in biblical Aramaic'.
new_statements.identity_note: JBA is an extinct, text-attested language (Babylonian Talmud, geonic literature). Every stress statement therefore concerns either a reading tradition or a reconstruction. Levias 1900 describes the 'traditional pronunciation' of the Talmud as known to him (the European/Ashkenazi reading tradition, not the Yemenite one studied later by Morag). Margolis 1910 (p. 15) takes the opposite stance and simply presupposes the Biblical Aramaic accent rules, admitting a shift may have occurred. The modern reference grammar (Bar-Asher Siegal 2013, ch. 4 §4.1, snippet only) treats the historical shift of stress from ultima to penult as the likely cause of final-vowel apocope in JBA (shared with Syriac and Mandaic). Glottolog's refs Vilsker 1981 (Samaritan Aramaic), Michelson 1909 and Andersen 1980 (Asoka edicts) and Jongeling et al. 1991 (syntax Festschrift) are misattached to jewi1240 and irrelevant.
